title: Keralam High Court Orders ₹9.73 Crore Released for 225 Victim Compensation Claims
excerpt: A Division Bench gave the Additional Chief Secretary (Home) five weeks to release the money, ordered KeLSA to review disbursements weekly, and told district authorities to collect victims' documents during their cases to prevent payment delays.
body:
• The Keralam High Court has directed the Additional Chief Secretary (Home) to release ₹9.73 crore to settle 225 victim compensation claims within five weeks.
  • A Division Bench of Chief Justice Soumen Sen and Justice V.M. Syam Kumar ordered the Kerala State Legal Services Authority (KeLSA) to review disbursement status with district legal services authorities every week.
  • District legal services authority secretaries must collect all required documents from victims while their cases are pending, to stop paperwork delays in payment.
  • The court also directed the State government to release mediator honorarium at revised rates, in the same suo motu case over delayed payments and mediation-centre infrastructure.

The Keralam High Court has directed the State government to release ₹9.73 crore to settle 225 pending victim compensation claims within five weeks, putting a deadline and a weekly monitoring mechanism on money that victims have been waiting for.

A Division Bench comprising Chief Justice Soumen Sen and Justice V.M. Syam Kumar directed the Additional Chief Secretary (Home) to release the amount, according to The Hindu. The Bench directed the Member Secretary of the Kerala State Legal Services Authority (KeLSA) to review the status of disbursements with the respective District Legal Services Authorities on a weekly basis.

Removing the Paperwork Bottleneck

The court also addressed a practical cause of delay. It directed the secretaries of the respective District Legal Services Authorities to collect all required documents from victims while their cases were pending before the court, so that missing paperwork does not hold up processing and payment after compensation is awarded. For a claimant, that is the actionable part of the order: documents are to be gathered during the case, not chased after it, and anyone with a pending claim should make sure their district legal services authority has their complete papers on file.

In a connected matter, the court took note of the revised honorarium rates for mediators at the Kerala State Mediation and Conciliation Centre and directed the State government to release the honorarium payable to mediators at the revised rates. The two matters were linked, the court noted, because both concerned delay in the release of payments by the State government.

A Case Built on Repeated Delays

The order came as the court reviewed a status report filed by KeLSA on the victim compensation scheme in a suo motu petition concerning inadequate infrastructure in mediation and alternative dispute resolution centres across the state. That same case has produced a series of increasingly sharp interventions. Earlier this year, as LiveLaw reported, the State told the court it had authorised ₹36.50 crore to clear victim compensation arrears and ₹12.26 crore towards arrears in mediator fees, after the Bench warned it could attach the State's treasury accounts if the money was not released within a week.

In that earlier hearing, the State's affidavit said the government was only one among several contributors to the victim compensation fund, that the fund had not been operationalised in the eight years since the rules were framed, and that the State had been meeting victim compensation expenditure from its own resources, which the Finance Department said it could not sustain indefinitely. The new order narrows the focus from the fund's overall arrears to a specific, countable set: 225 claims, ₹9.73 crore, five weeks.

What Happens Next

The weekly review the Bench ordered gives the case a built-in check. KeLSA's Member Secretary must track disbursement district by district, rather than the court discovering at a later hearing that authorisation and payment were different things — the gap that has defined this litigation. If the five-week deadline is met, 225 victims receive compensation that court orders had already awarded in principle. If it is missed, the State returns to a Bench that has previously raised treasury attachment in this same matter.

The order does not create a new compensation scheme or change eligibility. It enforces payment under the existing victim compensation framework, administered through KeLSA and the district legal services authorities, and it treats delayed payment itself — not the award — as the problem to be fixed.
